newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish shares lower on Iraqi tension.
newsitem.headline: Turkish shares lower on Iraqi tension.

text.p: Istanbul shares clawed back early losses caused by U.S. missile strikes against Iraqi military targets on Tuesday, but the market remained cautious, awaiting U.S. President Bill Clinton's statement, brokers said.

"It was normal for the shock fall to be followed by reaction buys because of cheap prices. But the duration of the Iraqi crisis will be important (for the market) from now on," said Bihlun Tamayligil from Deha securities.
The IMKB-100 market index which sank 2.2 percent to a low of 61,922 at the opening on news of the missile strikes, ended the morning session at 62,547.65, down 1.15 percent from Monday.
It had shed 1.95 percent on Monday in a negative mood prompted by weekend fighting in the Kurdish-held northern Iraq.
Brokers said morning volume remained thin at 2.4 trillion lira ($27 million) amid uncertainty over the new Iraqi tension.

U.S. navy warships in the Gulf and B-52 bombers fired 27 cruise missiles on air defence and military command and communications facilities in southern Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi miliary attacks against Kurds in the north.
The U.S. raid lasted about an hour.
Brokers said the market now awaited statements from U.S. and Turkish leaders after early fears of the U.S. base of Incirlik in southern Turkey being used for air strikes faded.
The Incirlik base was used for U.S. attacks on Iraq during the Gulf War in 1991.
"Uncertainty over the situation in Iraq is blocking cash entry to the market. But the index may still find a balance at around 62,500," said Koray Cervatoglu from Baran securities.
Bankers said Turkey's financial markets were quiet so far after the missile attacks.
"Some customers who were worried by the recent developments were buying hard currencies, but there was no negative reaction from banks," said a private bank dealer.
The Turkish lira weakened to 86,985 against the dollar at noon from Monday's 86,760 close in line with the dollar's gains against the mark in world markets.
Overnight money rates were little changed at 74.5 percent as cash demand persisted.
Treasury bill yields dropped by between one and two percentage points across the board as the market concentrated on the Treasury's bill auction rather than the missile attacks on Iraq.
